To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

long-term synaptic plasticity in the optic tectal synapses is retrogradely propagated to retinal synapses and that this retrograde spread is dependent on brain-derived neurotrophin and nitric oxide signaling.
LTP and/or LTD induced in the optic tectal synapses spread retrogradely to the retina, and that this retrograde spread is required for normal development of the visual system.
long-term potentiation and depression induced at the optic tectal synapses spread to the retinal synapses of the bipolar cells in a long-range retrograde manner.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how the brain processes information, and how the brain changes itself in response to the information.
the long-term effects of neural activity on the brain and how the brain can use these effects to change the way it functions.
how neural networks are organized in the nervous system, how they develop and how they change in response to experience.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the retrograde spread of long-term potentiation and depression is a novel mechanism of synaptic plasticity that may play a role in the development and function of neural circuits.
LTP and/or LTD can be retrogradely transmitted from one synapse to another, but the mechanisms of retrograde spread are different for LTP and LTD.
the retrograde spread of synaptic plasticity in the visual system may be a fundamental mechanism underlying the development of visual functions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the LTP and LTD at the retinotectum can be retrogradely propagated to the retina to adjust the strength of the input synapses on bipolar cells, and that the retrograde spread of these synaptic plasticity is mediated by BDNF and NO in the tectal cells.

the LTP/LTD induced in the optic tectal neurons can be retrogradely spread to the retina, which can be used to adjust the strength of the input synapses in the retina in accordance to the strength of the output synapses in the tectal neurons.
LTP and/or LTD can retrogradely spread to adjacent synpases, resulting in the long-range coordination of synaptic strengths in neural circuits.
The main takeaway from our work is that
LTP and LTP can be retrogradely spread to the presynaptic side of synapses in vivo.
the strength of synaptic connections between neurons can be adjusted in a coordinated manner, not only in the direction of information flow, but also in the opposite direction.
LTP and/or LTD can be retrogradely spread from the tectum to retinal bipolar cells, and that this retrograde spread requires the release of BDNF and NO in the tectal neurons.
